My opinions:

Where this article describes the safekeeping of what I like to call "cultural jewels", I'd like to express that cultural jewels are only kept through the efforts and in the heart of those who give them due attention. As a generalization, it appears to me that these things arent being lost so specifically through interconnectedness, but through neglect and discarding by the jewel inheriters. A "symptom of a deeper issue," is how I view it. Specifically, such an occasion could arise out of a native African persueing a relationship with an Asian. The man could feel inclined to develop alongside her for countless reasons, let's say lust for her physical form. That lust tips the scale of his thinking, it drives him to neglect the aspects of his cultural heritage, and adopt aspects that he believes she embodies, that are in contradiction to the preservation of his cultural jewels. You could easily say "See, had an Asian woman not been integrated into his community, this man would've prolonged the traditions!"

It doesn't appear to me that he would have. Had he not lusted for her, he probably would have acted out on, focused on, another stimulus. If he wants to practice and prioritize his cultural jewels, he will. If he wants to make efforts in seeking such jewels, he will. If he doesn't wish to do these things, it doesn't particularly imply fault on what he does instead of these things, or imply fault on the existence of other options he can choose. If this man strives to think critically and rationally, he can in time easily discern that certain cultural jewels are of great value and derived from the wisdom of his people. If he acts impulsively, he will probably throw out each and every jewel as he finds immediate benefit to do so, regardless of potential value of said jewel.

This essay says that each religion, custom, tradition, arises out of their blood and soil, and as such can't be made universal. Perhaps there is truth to this, but on a grander scale, I feel that each religion, custom, tradition arises out of people, and people are a universal phenomenon. People interacting with their context, context being another phenomena universal to our experience. When you have two people, three people, you have double context, triple context, regardless of the physical roots of said context. Those contexts are born of witness to, generally, love and unlove, and whichever way each specific traditon sways can always be discerned through patience, critical thinking, assessment, aka practice, when brought from the individuals heart. At that point, a person can be truly assured in the fact that their tradition, however cumulative or isolated, is good of itself, and as such, would never be served well through limiting. Or that the tradition is negative of a myriad of aspects, and that if they are seeking to exonerate a generalized level of goodness in their self, to hold to said tradition could serve as contradiction to their efforts.

I believe this essay expressed it's goals out of love, kudos to this fact. However, I don't believe in diversity simply for diversities sake, only as an aspect of protecting peoples right to learn from their context, so as to gain insight in a way molded to there experience. I think this essay comes from a degree of not seeing the big picture, something I am fully in lack of myself.

It amazes me how the industry (and many of the players, myself included) fail to tire of "zombie survival."

The thing is that 'zombie survival' is a description that fits a lot of fundamentally different games.

There's just a lot of places you can go when creating a game in this setting. Sure most go for the action route which is overdone, but not all do. Look at Project Zomboid for a game that focuses on the survival aspect.

I'd love a game that focuses on the emotional drama for a change. I mean, just forget about all the zombie games for a moment think about the concept of a zombie apocalypse for a moment; The implications.

Behind every single mindless zombie you kill with glee in your average zombie shooter, there's a story waiting to be told.

The terror of leaving your safe house to get food. The constant fear that it might not be as safe as you think it is. Knowing that your luck WILL change sooner or later. Project Zomboid nails the struggle of survival down like a champ.

Now make me care about the characters...

What about a zombie game that starts way before the apocalypse? A game that establishes characters and makes me care about them? A game where everything going to hell would have some impact for a change? A game that portays the zombie apocalypse as what it really would be like: An apocalypse. There isn't anything cool or badass about living through the apocalypse. Even if you did something incredibly cool, nobody would have seen and there wouldn't be anyone you could tell.

That's the zombie game I'm waiting for...

Zombies are just a generic hazard, people like them because they're scary, numerous, and dangerous. You could replace them with robots or monsters and get the same effect. It's surviving after the apocalypse that's got people really hooked.

Not quite. There's a romantic aspect to zombies because of the "these were all once people" aspect which can lead to great drama as soon in TWD and other well-done zombie-oriented media. There's not a whole lot of "robot survival" out there. In fact, a Matrix-y open world survival game sounds pretty frickin' awesome.
